subjects.displayTitle: Steadfastness, perseverance and faithfulness: firmly settled as the immovable mountain
subjects.introduction: Bahá’u’lláh calls steadfastness the crown of all deeds and records that the first word His Pen set down in the Crimson Book was steadfastness in the Cause. It is a striking primacy for a virtue that can look like merely staying put. Yet He defines it as knowing God alone as the One who prevails over all things and seeing everything else as passing; to stand firm is to have settled what is real. The believer is asked to be as firmly settled as the immovable mountain, outwardly unmoved and inwardly a surging ocean, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that to enter the Kingdom is easy while to remain is hard, since many take ten steps and stop. Firmness in safety, he observes, is something even a weak ant can manage; it is the winds of tests and trials that show which tree is rooted. Those winds lead inward to patience, onward to the lifelong loyalty that is firmness in the Covenant, and at last to trust in God, the ground on which a soul can stand when everything else gives way.

order.why: These readings begin with the place steadfastness holds in the Faith. Bahá’u’lláh records that the first word written by the Supreme Pen in the Crimson Book was steadfastness in the Cause, and that the first counsel enjoined upon His loved ones in the Book is the Most Great Steadfastness; in the Tajallíyát it is the second effulgence. He calls it the crown of all deeds, a jewel the gems of the world cannot equal, a garment more beauteous than any other and the essence of all essences, whose value no writer can describe, and He says that were the station of one steadfast soul disclosed, all would be thunderstruck. The Báb cites the Qur’anic promise that angels descend upon those who say ‘Our Lord is God’ and then remain steadfast, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá repeats it, calling steadfastness the greatest attribute of the human world, the magnet of divine bounties and the greatest miracle. A reported talk recalls Muhammad’s saying that the verse of steadfastness made Him old. The promise is assistance: no steadfast one has been deprived, and what befits God is grace and reward.

This section asks what steadfastness is and how it is gained. Bahá’u’lláh defines it as knowing God alone as the One who prevails over all things and seeing all else as evanescent, and as being independent of all save God. The beginning of the matter is the recognition of God and its end is steadfastness in His Cause; once that station is reached, steadfastness is one of two things obligatory on every soul. True listening, He writes, is to hear the call of the All-Merciful and then remain so steadfast that the denial of all peoples could not deflect one from the straight path, and a prayer adds that none can stand firm save one detached from all else. He bids the friends reflect upon its degrees and seek it with lowliness. order.why: This section takes up the tests that make steadfastness visible. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that it is God’s way to test the sincere with great trials, that until fierce winds blow the firm tree cannot be told from the unstable one, and that firmness in comfort and safety is something even a weak ant can manage, while skill shows when the captain steers through the storm. Gold melted in the fire, a diamond under the millstone, a candle shining while an owl hides in a dark corner: such are his images for those who stand. Bahá’u’lláh observes how many strong souls wavered when the winds of tests blew and how many weak ones were made steadfast, how leaves fell from the tree of His Cause while others clung to it, and how strange it is that those who claim steadfastness are shaken by the merest whiff of vain imaginings. Reported talks add that without trials nothing is accomplished and that a different spirituality appears in one who remains firm. The Báb bids the believer let nothing destined in this Cause disturb him.
shortened: Thus We call unto thee from beyond the sea of grandeur, upon the crimson land, above the horizon of tribulation. Verily, no God is there save Him, the Almighty, the Most Generous. Walk thou steadfastly in My Cause and follow not the ways of those who, upon attaining unto the object of their desire, denied God, the Lord of Lords.

Patience is the inward side of steadfastness, and this section gathers counsels on it. In the Súriy-i-Haykal Bahá’u’lláh recalls that He withstood His trials with forbearance and enjoined patience and fortitude on God’s servants. He bids the believer be patient even as his Lord was patient, and then yet more patient, for the end is for such as endure with constancy; this, He says, is the day of patience, and the loved ones should cling to the hem of patience through His Name, the All-Patient. The Báb calls for beautiful patience and recalls the promise that those patient under the words of enemies receive the reward of a thousand martyrs. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes believers whose patience did not fail though their hearts burned, who were steadfast upon burning coals, and who in affliction comforted others, their faces glowing with radiant acquiescence. He calls the shirt of patience the most adorning garment, quotes the saying that the patient are rewarded while God’s decree is done either way, and tells how his own trials passed away through patience and calm.
shortened: We withstood all these trials with forbearance, and enjoined upon God's servants to show forth patience and fortitude.  Removing Ourself from their midst, We took up residence in another house, that perchance the flame of envy might be quenched in Our brother's breast, and that he might be guided aright.

He bids the believer be patient even as his Lord was patient, and then yet more patient, for the end is for such as endure with constancy; this, He says, is the day of patience, and the loved ones should cling to the hem of patience through His Name, the All-Patient. The Báb calls for beautiful patience and recalls the promise that those patient under the words of enemies receive the reward of a thousand martyrs. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes believers whose patience did not fail though their hearts burned, who were steadfast upon burning coals, and who in affliction comforted others, their faces glowing with radiant acquiescence. He calls the shirt of patience the most adorning garment, quotes the saying that the patient are rewarded while God’s decree is done either way, and tells how his own trials passed away through patience and calm.

order.why: Steadfastness in the Writings is first of all steadfastness in love. In the Hidden Words the sign of love is fortitude under God’s decree and patience under His trials, and in the Lawh-i-Ahmad Bahá’u’lláh asks that the believer be so steadfast in His love that the heart shall not waver though the swords of the enemies rain blows; the same Tablet bids him rely upon God. He names steadfastness in His love as the first of what is required, a steadfastness that takes no account of enemy or pretender, and says it endures even should one find oneself alone in love for one’s Lord. Prayers and passages in His own voice add that in God’s love every fire is light and every sorrow gladness, that none of the kings of the earth can hinder Him from extolling God, and that His soul would not be emptied of love were He slain; in the Fire Tablet He has risen up in faithfulness at the place of sacrifice. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks the friends to accept every tribulation in their love for God, and his verses vow not to turn away whatever fire, blood or prison may come.
shortened: For everything there is a sign. The sign of love is fortitude under My decree and patience under My trials.

Rely upon God, thy God and the Lord of thy fathers. For the people are wandering in the paths of delusion, bereft of discernment to see God with their own eyes, or hear His Melody with their own ears. Thus have We found them, as thou also dost witness.

Steadfastness rests on trust, and this section gathers counsels on reliance upon God. In the Súriy-i-Mulúk Bahá’u’lláh bids the believer place his whole trust in his Lord in all circumstances and not rely on his treasures, and in the Words of Wisdom He names trust in God, submission to His command and contentment with His pleasure as the source of all good. He writes that it is incumbent on every man to trust in God’s bounties and arise to teach His Cause, that one must lift the gaze from outward causes, and that if outward means fail one should not be disheartened, since every matter has its appointed time. A leaf, He says, moves only with the divine breeze, so an opposer might better try to stop the winds; fear and anxiety do not befit the people of truth. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá bids the friends rely upon God, Who turns trouble into ease, never lose hope, since man is immersed in a sea of His blessings, and never let outward circumstances worry them. In a reported talk he says that he has been under God’s protection from the day he was born.
shortened: The day is approaching when God will have exalted His Cause and magnified His testimony in the eyes of all who are in the heavens and all who are on the earth. Place, in all circumstances, Thy whole trust in Thy Lord, and fix Thy gaze upon Him, and turn away from all them that repudiate His truth. Let God, Thy Lord, be Thy sufficing succourer and helper.

Place not thy reliance on thy treasures. Put thy whole confidence in the grace of God, thy Lord. Let Him be thy trust in whatever thou doest, and be of them that have submitted themselves to His Will.

This section gathers accounts of believers who stood firm in life and in death. In the Lawh-i-Ra’ís Bahá’u’lláh says of His companions that their blood implores to be spilt in His path, and in another Tablet He tells of a mother who urged her son to offer himself in the path of God and not betray his faith; His recorded recollections of imprisonment tell of fellow-prisoners who bore hunger without a murmur. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, in the Memorials of the Faithful and in Tablets, writes of an enraptured lover of God who never gave way, of the martyrs of Yazd and Isfahan whose steadfastness is the greatest proof of the friends’ sincerity, of prisoners from whom no moan was heard, of the loved ones of Nayriz, of the steadfast believers of London, and of women who outstripped men in the arena of firmness. Reported talks tell of the besieged in the fortress who ate the leather of their shoes, of the martyrs of Yazd who did not defend themselves, and of Persian believers who cried ‘Yá Bahá’u’l-Abhá!’ under the sword, and they contrast Peter’s denial with the constancy of the followers of Bahá’u’lláh.
shortened: These souls have never held, nor shall they ever hold any grievance.  Nay, their blood continually imploreth and beseecheth the Lord of the worlds that it might be spilt upon the dust in His path, and their heads yearn to be borne aloft on spears for the sake of the Beloved of hearts and souls.

They bless His loved ones whom the changes and chances of the world have not deterred, whom adversities cannot estrange from His Cause, and who under the blaze of His trials have clung to the cord of patience. They ask that the doubts of the infidels not keep the believer back, that hearts be so strengthened that the power of the unbelievers will not frighten them, and that the friends be endued with such constancy that they arise to proclaim His Cause before all. One confesses that there is no refuge to flee to except God. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that the friends be made like firmly-fixed mountains in the Covenant, unshaken by storms, and presents a servant passionately wandering in the desert of God’s love.

They ask that the doubts of the infidels not keep the believer back, that hearts be so strengthened that the power of the unbelievers will not frighten them, and that the friends be endued with such constancy that they arise to proclaim His Cause before all. One confesses that there is no refuge to flee to except God. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that the friends be made like firmly-fixed mountains in the Covenant, unshaken by storms, and presents a servant passionately wandering in the desert of God’s love.
shortened: Endue them, then, with such constancy that they will arise to proclaim Thy Cause, and will call on Thy name, before all that are in Thy heaven and on Thy earth, in such wise that the Pharaohic cruelties inflicted by the oppressors among Thy servants will not succeed in keeping them back from Thee.

In these authorized words of Bahá’u’lláh, found in Gleanings CLXII, the Pen of the Most High blesses him whom the changes and chances of this world have failed to deter from recognizing the Dayspring of the Unity of God, and who has quaffed with unswerving resolve the sealed wine of His Revelation. In the catalogue record the paragraph goes on to say that such a one shall be numbered with the inmates of Paradise. The supplied extract differs from the authorized text only in spelling Dayspring as two words, and keeps its approximate status. It belongs beside the readings on the station of steadfastness and on tests.

This supplied extract from Gleanings CXXXIV joins two passages of Bahá’u’lláh. Its first sentence, He, verily, shall increase the reward of them that endure with patience, closes a paragraph of the Súriy-i-Mulúk in which He speaks of His own persevering patience under tribulation. The rest lists the virtues and attributes pertaining unto God that are mentioned in all the heavenly Books, among them forbearance, resignation, contentment, patience and thankfulness in the midst of tribulation, and complete reliance upon Him. Because the two parts come from different contexts, the extract keeps its approximate status. It extends the section on patience.

This supplied sentence comes from a letter written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi on 27 June 1942. It calls perseverance the magnet that will, in these days, attract the promised blessings of the Almighty Author of the Faith. The image echoes ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s description, in the opening section, of steadfastness as the magnet of divine bounties, and it joins the readings on perseverance in effort and service. No catalogue record was supplied, so the wording keeps its unmatched status.

This supplied sentence, cited from Gleanings CXV, promises: Supremely lofty will be thy station, if thou remainest steadfast in the Cause of thy Lord. The catalogue’s record of the Tablet, addressed to Dhabíh, carries the same promise in a provisional rendering that lies outside its authorized paragraphs, in a passage where Bahá’u’lláh calls for a penetrating vision, a steadfast heart and legs of brass. The supplied wording keeps its approximate status. It belongs with the opening readings on the station and reward of steadfastness.

This supplied passage comes from a letter written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi on 31 March 1932. It suggests that a believer may have achieved little in teaching because he looked at his own weaknesses, and recalls that Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urged the friends to disregard their handicaps and lay their whole reliance upon God, Who will come to the help of those who arise. Teachers, it says, are pure souls who take the first step and let the spirit of Bahá’u’lláh make use of them. No catalogue record was supplied, so the wording keeps its unmatched status. It completes the section on trust.
shortened: Baha'u'llah and the Master have both urged us repeatedly to disregard our own handicaps and lay our whole reliance upon God. He will come to our help if we only arise and become an active channel for God's grace. Do you think it is the teachers who make converts and change human hearts? No, surely not. They are only pure souls who take the first step, and then let the spirit of Baha'u'llah move them and make use of them.

order.why: This supplied passage of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá is cited from The Advent of Divine Justice, where Shoghi Effendi quotes it. It says that the powers of the leaders of religion are directed towards the dispersion of the congregation of the All-Merciful and that material, cultural and political forces assault the Cause from every side, so that all who shelter beneath God’s providence must show such steadfastness as will astound the minds of all. The catalogue record of the Tablet is not authorized and its provisional rendering differs, so the supplied wording keeps its approximate status. It joins the readings on firmness in the Covenant and on tests.

questions: Bahá’u’lláh calls steadfastness the first word of the Crimson Book and the crown of all deeds, yet also the end of a matter whose beginning is the recognition of God. How do the opening sections help you understand why steadfastness, and not recognition alone, is given such a station?

Bahá’u’lláh defines steadfastness as knowing God alone as the One who prevails over all things, while ‘Abdu’l-Bahá names silence, contentment, deeds and self-sacrifice as its causes and evidence. Which of these seems most within reach in your own circumstances, and why?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that firmness in safety is something even a weak ant can manage, and a reported talk says that without trials nothing is accomplished. Using the sections on mountains, trees and tests, consider how trials reveal steadfastness and how they build it.

The Hidden Words call fortitude under God’s decree the sign of love, and several passages say that in His love every fire is light. How does the section on steadfastness in love change the way the section on patience reads?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá tells the friends that even if he were raised upon the gallows, or news came that the Holy Land had changed, they must grow firmer, and that the condition of steadfastness is following in all things. What do the readings on the Covenant and on faithfulness suggest steadfastness is anchored to?

Several readings say that to enter the Kingdom is easy but to remain is hard, and that many take ten steps and stop. Choose one account from the section on those who stood firm and one counsel on perseverance, and consider what they suggest about steadfastness over the length of a life.
